experiment_plans.feasibility_notes: The hypothesis is feasible given available data and compute resources. We will use the Fama-French three-factor data and a synthetic news headline dataset (from AG News) to simulate sentiment analysis. Since we don't have a real financial news dataset with labeled sentiment, we will generate synthetic sentiment labels based on the AG News headlines using a pre-trained BERT model. This allows us to test the core idea without requiring access to a large, labeled financial news dataset.
experiment_plans.objective: To determine whether a BERT-based financial sentiment model trained on news headlines improves next-day directional prediction of S&P 500 returns compared to a model using only Fama-French three-factor risk premiums, using Granger causality tests.

independent: BERT-based sentiment scores from news headlines
dependent: Next-day directional prediction of S&P 500 returns

experiment_plans.design: Comparative benchmark experiment using Granger causality tests to evaluate the predictive power of two models: one based on BERT sentiment scores and another based on Fama-French factors. Both models predict the direction of next-day S&P 500 returns.

data_requirements.description: AG News dataset containing real news headlines and descriptions. We will use this to generate synthetic financial sentiment labels for news headlines, simulating a financial news dataset. The dataset provides 120,000 short news articles categorized by topic.
preprocessing_steps: Load the AG News train dataset
Extract text column for headline generation
Apply BERT-based sentiment analysis to generate synthetic sentiment scores
Merge sentiment scores with Fama-French factor data
Align dates to create time series for Granger causality testing

methods.name: BERT-based models
methods.description: Use a pre-trained BERT model fine-tuned for financial sentiment analysis to score news headlines. In this case, we'll apply a general-purpose BERT model to generate sentiment scores for the AG News headlines, treating them as if they were financial news. The model outputs a sentiment score for each headline that represents the degree of positive/negative sentiment.

methods.name: Granger causality analysis
methods.description: Apply Granger causality tests to determine whether past values of one variable (sentiment scores or Fama-French factors) help predict future values of another variable (next-day S&P 500 return direction). This involves fitting autoregressive models and testing statistical significance of lagged predictors.

evaluation.baseline: Model using only Fama-French three-factor risk premiums
evaluation.success_criteria: If the BERT-based sentiment model shows higher Granger causality F-statistics or greater directional prediction accuracy than the Fama-French model, the hypothesis is supported. If not, the hypothesis is refuted.

implementation_steps.description: Load the AG News train dataset (ag_news_document_text_category_classification_train.csv) and extract the text column for headline generation.
Download and initialize a pre-trained BERT model for sentiment analysis (e.g., bert-base-uncased with a sentiment classification head).
Generate synthetic sentiment scores for all AG News headlines using the BERT model, treating them as financial news.
Load the Fama-French three-factor daily returns dataset (fama_french_three_factor_daily_returns.csv) and convert percentage returns to decimal form.
Align the sentiment scores and Fama-French factors by date to create a unified time series dataset for analysis.
Create a binary indicator for next-day S&P 500 return direction (positive/negative) from the historical stock market data.
Implement Granger causality tests for both models: one using BERT sentiment scores and one using Fama-French factors to predict next-day return direction.
Compare the F-statistics from the Granger causality tests to determine which model has stronger predictive power.

risks: Synthetic sentiment labels may not accurately reflect real financial sentiment
The alignment of dates between sentiment data and financial data might introduce timing mismatches
Granger causality tests assume linear relationships, which may not hold for financial data
